draft.title: Graphs of logarithmic functions
card: The graph of y = log_a(x) is the reflection of y = aˣ in the line y = x. Swapping x and y turns each point (p, q) on one graph into (q, p) on the other.
The y-intercept of y = aˣ is (0, 1), so y = log_a(x) passes through (1, 0). It has no y-intercept.
The horizontal asymptote y = 0 of y = aˣ becomes a vertical asymptote x = 0. The graph only exists for x > 0, because you cannot raise a positive base to a power and get zero or a negative number.
Example: 2³ = 8 puts (3, 8) on y = 2ˣ, so (8, 3) is on y = log₂(x). For a > 1 the graph rises. Its gradient is steep near x = 0 and flattens as x grows.
draft.remember: y = log_a(x) is y = aˣ reflected in y = x: through (1, 0), with a vertical asymptote at x = 0.

a.q: Which point lies on the graph of y = log₃(x)?
a.why: 3² = 9, so log₃ 9 = 2 and (9, 2) is on the graph. (2, 9) has the coordinates the wrong way round: it lies on y = 3ˣ's reflection partner, not on this graph.
a.clue: Reflecting in y = x swaps the coordinates of a point on y = 3ˣ.

b.q: The graph of y = log₂(x) is reflected in the line y = x to give another graph. Which statement about y = log₂(x) is correct?
opts: It has a vertical asymptote at x = 0
It has a horizontal asymptote at y = 0
It is defined for all real values of x
b.why: The horizontal asymptote y = 0 of y = 2ˣ reflects into the vertical line x = 0. The graph does not have a y-intercept at (0, 1): that belongs to y = 2ˣ, and the logarithm passes through (1, 0) instead.
b.clue: Reflecting in y = x swaps x and y, so a horizontal line becomes a vertical line.

b.best: It has a vertical asymptote at x = 0

problems.detail: The why says (2, 9) 'lies on y = 3ˣ's reflection partner, not on this graph'. That is wrong: (2, 9) lies on y = 3ˣ itself, and the reflection partner of y = 3ˣ is y = log₃(x), which is this graph. The explanation contradicts itself and the card.

The stem first says y = log₂(x) is reflected in y = x to give another graph, then asks about y = log₂(x) itself. The reflection sentence plays no part in the question and may make students think they should be describing the reflected graph (y = 2ˣ), where 'horizontal asymptote at y = 0' and 'y-intercept at (0, 1)' would be correct.

final.title: Graphs of logarithmic functions
card: The graph of \(y = \log_{a}(x)\) is the reflection of \(y = a^{x}\) in the line \(y = x\). Swapping \(x\) and \(y\) turns each point \((p, q)\) on one graph into \((q, p)\) on the other.
The y-intercept of \(y = a^{x}\) is \((0, 1)\), so \(y = \log_{a}(x)\) passes through \((1, 0)\). It has no y-intercept.

The horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\) of \(y = a^{x}\) becomes a vertical asymptote \(x = 0\). The graph only exists for \(x > 0\), because a positive base raised to any power never gives zero or a negative number.
Example: \(2^{3} = 8\) puts \((3, 8)\) on \(y = 2^{x}\), so \((8, 3)\) is on \(y = \log_{2}(x)\). For \(a > 1\) the graph rises. Its gradient is steep near \(x = 0\) and flattens as \(x\) grows.

1.alt: The graphs of \(y = 2^{x}\) and \(y = \log_{2}(x)\), reflections of each other in the dotted line \(y = x\). The point \((0, 1)\) on \(y = 2^{x}\) matches \((1, 0)\) on the log graph, and \((2, 4)\) matches \((4, 2)\).

final.remember: Swap the coordinates of \(y = a^{x}\) to get the log graph: through \((1, 0)\), with a vertical asymptote at \(x = 0\).

a.q: Which point lies on the graph of \(y = \log_{3}(x)\)?
a.why: \(3^{2} = 9\), so \(\log_{3} 9 = 2\) and \((9, 2)\) is on the graph. \((2, 9)\) lies on \(y = 3^{x}\) itself. Reflecting it in \(y = x\) swaps the coordinates and gives \((9, 2)\) on \(y = \log_{3}(x)\).
a.clue: Find a point on \(y = 3^{x}\), then swap its coordinates.

b.q: Which statement about the graph of \(y = \log_{2}(x)\) is correct?
opts: It has a vertical asymptote at \(x = 0\)
It has a horizontal asymptote at \(y = 0\)
It is defined for all real values of \(x\)
b.why: The horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\) of \(y = 2^{x}\) reflects into the vertical line \(x = 0\). A horizontal asymptote at \(y = 0\) and a y-intercept at \((0, 1)\) are features of \(y = 2^{x}\), not of the log graph, which passes through \((1, 0)\) and exists only for \(x > 0\).
b.clue: Reflecting in \(y = x\) swaps \(x\) and \(y\), so a horizontal line becomes a vertical line.
